rv.q: As embodied by a brilliant Ethan Hawke, in full-menace mode, and a tightly wired Paul Dano, everyday sibling rivalry has seldom felt this ominous.
The production, directed by James Macdonald, is a master class in how to stage Shepard'
The production succeeds largely because of the ferocious commitment of its two leads, Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano.
Hawke, of course, lives for this type of juicy role, playing dirty in more ways than one.
Shepard’s play is symbolic and strange, if also a bit thin.
But it works marvelously as a mood piece, which for several reasons this production only partially succeeds in capturing.
But up inside its jewel box, so neatly delineated and so separate from us, the mess this production makes is largely artificial, well designed but not dangerous.
In other words, this is the most well-behaved True West I’ve ever seen.
Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano duke it out as battling brothers in a disappointing revival of Sam Shepard’s fierce 1980 classic.

For this production, the Roundabout, under James Macdonald’s direction, has brought together Ethan Hawke and Paul Dano, who somehow produce all the great upheaval of a 10-gallon hat left out in a drizzle.
Hoffman and Reilly, regardless of the role each is playing at the moment, transcend the limits of this production, and make True West one of the few 'must see' plays of this season.
Both stars deliver top-caliber work.
Hawke and Dano — do an excellent job going round for round, playing into the comedic moments of their fighting.
In elder brother Lee, a drifter and thief, Hawke has found a vehicle for both his comedic facility (not always mined or guided adroitly, on stage or screen) and his capacity for menace.

The play, about a pair of estranged brothers and their apparent role reversal under pressure, is as funny as it is serious, and this new staging, directed by James Macdonald, a specialist in heavy-hitters, is as entertaining as it is profound.
Dano's paralytic letting-go is wonderful—a cavalcade of clowning, pratfalls, and jerky limbs—because what’s more funny than a fuddy-duddy going loco?
Hawke and Dano aren’t even distant cousins.
This new version, directed by James Macdonald, could use a high-voltage power infusion.
People will go to see Ethan Hawke, and there are moments when he does not disappoint.
But star-power short-circuits in this curiously light-hearted production from director James Macdonald at the Theatre.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this Roundabout revival of Shepard's classic, with Hawke's fierce performance earning widespread praise while Dano draws mixed reactions and the production itself deemed uneven.
